Ukraine: Russian strikes hit the Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv, Paris calls for a UN Security Council meeting

A day after the Russian attack that killed six people in Kyiv and sent missiles into Poland, France is calling for a UN Security Council meeting: the Austrian and Dutch embassies were damaged. NATO chief Mark Rutte is expected in Warsaw on Saturday [1][2][6].

Russian strikes overnight from Thursday to Friday killed six people in Kyiv, according to Euronews, and damaged two bridges, including the Podil-Voskresensky bridge, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko [1].
The Austrian and Dutch embassies were hit; France has requested a meeting of the United Nations Security Council [2].
Emmanuel Macron denounced Russia's “aggressive agenda” on “European territory” [3].
During the same attack, two missiles and a jet-powered drone came down in Poland [4]. A Kh-101 missile was found in the village of Nowy Lipowiec, in the east of the country; no one was injured [5].
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke of an “intentional provocation,” at a time when thousands of European soldiers were conducting unprecedented exercises in southeastern Poland [6].
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte denounced a “serious violation” of Polish airspace; according to Donald Tusk, he will be in Warsaw on Saturday. Moscow had not responded as of Friday evening [6].
Key takeaway: in a single night, the war reached both the soil of a NATO country and the diplomatic buildings of two EU countries, prompting Europeans to take the matter to the UN [2][4].

The timing matters: according to the Financial Times, cited by Il Sole 24 Ore, Donald Trump told the Europeans and Ukrainians that he wanted a peace deal by early January [7]. Every strike on European targets therefore weighs on the balance of power at the negotiating table.

For Poland, precedent counts: Warsaw can request consultations among allies under Article 4 of the NATO treaty, as it did last year [6]. Mark Rutte's visit is meant to allow discussion of a joint response, according to Donald Tusk [6].
The Security Council remains limited, however: Russia holds a veto there, so a meeting serves mainly as a means of diplomatic pressure.

France itself is pushing the issue at the UN: the security of Europe's eastern flank involves its soldiers, deployed in NATO exercises and missions. As for your wallet, every escalation around Ukraine increases the pressure to raise defense budgets, and therefore on public finances, including in France.

Cost of living: young people take to the streets in more than 25 European countries, France follows with an “Act VI” this Saturday

On Friday, November 20, young people demonstrated across Europe against the high cost of living, the cost of housing and education, and militarization, and are calling for more action. In France, an “Act VI” is planned for Saturday, while the bill for the October urban unrest exceeds €200 million [1][4][7].
On Friday, protesters, mostly young people, marched in many European countries against the cost of living, housing prices, study conditions and militarization [1][3].
According to the organizing coalition, youth rallies were planned in more than 25 countries [2]. At the end of the day, protesters called for the movement to continue [1].
This Saturday, November 21, the Yellow Vests are calling for an “Act VI” in France, and a march bringing together unions, student organizations and associations is planned in Paris [4].
The day is part of three days of action (November 20, 21 and 22) launched by unions and associations from seven European countries for the right to housing and against the high cost of living [4].

Outside Paris, a march leaves from Marseille at 2:30 p.m. [5]; in Saint-Nazaire, actions are announced near the Océanis shopping area from 2 p.m., while in Nantes the prefecture has banned undeclared gatherings in certain areas [6].
The urban unrest of October 17 and 18 is expected to cost more than €200 million: France Assureurs estimates insured damage at €207 million for 5,280 claims [7].

Key takeaway: French social anger is no longer isolated. On the same weekend, young people in more than 25 countries are highlighting the same issues: finding housing, studying, paying for groceries [1][2].
The movement links two debates: purchasing power and public money spent on defense. Protesters reject “militarization” at a time when European countries are increasing their military spending [1][3].

In France, the mobilization has lasted six weeks, as the name “Act VI” indicates [4]. It already has a measurable economic cost: €207 million in insured damage for the nights of October 17 and 18 alone, according to insurers [7]. These sums then end up in the insurance premiums of businesses and local authorities.
Authorities are wavering between supervision and local bans, as in Nantes, where undeclared gatherings are prohibited in several areas [6].

If you go out this weekend in Paris, Marseille, Nantes or Saint-Nazaire, expect marches and disruption in the early afternoon. More fundamentally, housing, energy and food are the items that weigh most on your budget: they are what the demands target.

Argentina: “country risk” tops 1,000 points for the first time in more than a year, the dollar hits a record against the peso

On Friday, November 20, the premium investors demand to lend to Argentina jumped to 1,065 points, according to broker Rava, its highest in more than a year. The dollar hit a nominal record against the peso. Economy Minister Luis Caputo blames the external shock and fears of a return of Kirchnerism [1][2][3].

The “riesgo país,” the gap between the rate at which Argentina borrows in dollars and the US rate, rose 134 points in one session to 1,065 points, according to Rava [1]. JP Morgan put it at 1,025 points, the highest in more than a year [3].
Government bonds lost up to 2.8%, and Argentine stocks about 3% in New York [1][6].
The dollar reached 1,600 pesos (selling rate) at Banco Nación counters, and the wholesale dollar, used by banks, hit a nominal record of 1,580 pesos [1][2]. The peso fell 0.9% on the day [6].
The 1,000-point threshold had not been crossed since October 2025 [1][3]. In early July 2026, the indicator had fallen to about 400 points, its lowest since 2018 [7].

Economy Minister Luis Caputo had blamed a “rather brutal external shock” in October (high global interest rates, expensive oil) [9]. On November 16, he added the “riesgo kuka,” the fear of a return of the Kirchnerists, which “weighs on the economy” [5].

According to Santiago Casas of the consultancy Ecoanalytics, the market is pricing in the political risk of the 2027 presidential election in advance [1][2]. Infobae notes that, behind the “riesgo kuka,” two other political concerns are growing [4].
The 2027 budget is due to be voted on by the lower house on November 25. It assumes 4% growth, 18% inflation and an official dollar at 1,847.60 pesos in December 2027 [8].
Key takeaway: in four months, Argentina's risk premium has more than doubled, erasing the main financial success of Javier Milei, who hoped to return to borrowing on international markets [3][7].

The higher this figure, the more the state, provinces and companies pay to borrow in dollars. Luis Caputo was aiming instead for 250 to 300 points before launching new international bond issues: the indicator is now more than three times higher [7][11].

The peso trades within a “band” published by the central bank (BCRA): on Friday, its reference ceiling was 1,976.68 pesos for the wholesale dollar, still far from the rate of 1,580 [10][1]. Pressure is therefore rising, without reaching the limit. But a weaker peso makes imported goods more expensive, while the budget is betting on inflation brought down to 18% in 2027 [8].

The political calendar weighs: investors are already comparing what bonds will be worth before and after the October 2027 presidential election [6]. The budget vote on November 25 will test Milei's ability to keep his allies [8].

If you travel to Argentina, a weakening peso makes the country cheaper when you pay in euros, but local prices can rise quickly. And if you hold “emerging market” funds, this drop shows how sensitive they are to politics.

Brazil: Lula signs the end of the six-day week, 14.8 million workers will get two days off from December 16

President Lula has signed the decree ending the “6x1” schedule (six days of work, one day off) in Brazil. From December 16, the maximum working week drops from 44 to 42 hours, then to 40 hours in December 2027, with no pay cut. Employers are challenging it before the Supreme Court [1][2][4].

Lula signed Decree No. 13.173/2026 on Thursday, November 19, at the Planalto Palace in Brasília; it was published in a special edition of the Official Gazette and implements Constitutional Amendment 141/2026, passed by Congress in October [1][2]. “What we are doing is humanizing the world of work,” the president said [1].
Timeline: the maximum working week drops from 44 to 42 hours on December 16, 2026, with two paid days off, one of them preferably on Sunday; the 40-hour cap will apply on December 16, 2027 [2][4].

According to the Labor Ministry, 14.8 million Brazilians who currently work six days a week are directly affected; 21.7 million others, already on five days but at 44 hours, will see their hours reduced [2][3].
Monthly pay does not change, but each hour is worth more: for 3,000 reais a month, it rises from 13.64 to 14.29 reais, according to the government, which makes overtime more expensive [1][7].

The employers' confederations for industry (CNI) and commerce (CNC) have appealed to the Supreme Court (STF). Justice Flávio Dino kept the start of the transition in December; the full court has yet to rule [2][5].
Lula responded to critics: in his view, rested workers “produce more” and modernization makes it possible to cut working time without economic losses; he nevertheless expects court battles [6][7].
The president was due to defend the measure on Saturday, November 21, in a social media livestream with lawmaker André Janones [8].
Key takeaway: the reform affects more than 36 million Brazilian workers, those who work six days a week and those who already work five days but 44 hours [2][3].

For businesses, especially retail, restaurants and services open seven days a week, it will mean hiring, reorganizing schedules or paying more overtime. That is why the CNI and CNC are trying to get the reform limited by the Supreme Court [2][5].

The decree allows some flexibility: eight days off per month instead of two per week, if a collective agreement provides for it [3]. Ministers Geraldo Alckmin and Luiz Marinho (Labor) stood beside Lula at the signing [3].

For comparison: in France, the legal working week is 35 hours; Brazil is moving from 44 to 40 hours in two stages. If you work for a French company operating in Brazil (retail, distribution, services), expect reorganizations there, and a debate about costs.

Gold: driven out of Guinea's mines, 76,169 artisanal miners return to Burkina, and Conakry cuts off Burkinabe public television

Burkina Faso announced on Friday, November 20, the end of the repatriation of artisanal gold miners expelled from Guinea: 76,169 people registered, including 15,968 children. The day before, Guinea's regulator had banned Burkinabe public television RTB after a caricature of President Mamadi Doumbouya. The battle for Siguiri's gold is turning into a crisis between neighbors [1][3].

In a statement on November 20, the Burkinabe government set the toll as of November 18: 76,169 people registered, including 15,968 children. The last convoy arrived overnight from November 18 to 19, and the reception sites in Bobo-Dioulasso and Koloko have closed [1].

These miners crossed Mali before being transferred to Burkina [1]. The count also includes 983 Togolese, 580 Beninese, 150 Ivorians, 133 Nigeriens and 44 Malians, for whom Ouagadougou is in talks with their embassies [1][2]; Togo began repatriating its nationals on Friday [10].

It all began on November 2: unregulated gold panning was banned in the Siguiri region, in northeastern Guinea, on the grounds of land and river pollution [5]. More than 1,200 people have been arrested, according to AFP, and clashes have left at least 10 dead and 13 injured, according to the government [5].

On November 19, Guinea's High Authority for Communication (HAC) banned RTB “until further notice,” in a decision signed by its president, Boubacar Yacine Diallo. It also ordered Canal+ Guinée to remove the channel from its packages [3][4].

The ban targets an editorial, “La caricature de Zoétaba : drôle de justice dans le royaume de l'or” (“The Zoétaba caricature: strange justice in the kingdom of gold”), illustrated with a drawing of Mamadi Doumbouya and deemed an affront to the president's honor [4]. Until then, Ouagadougou had described the operation as “very regrettable” [4].

On the Guinean side, Foreign Minister Morissanda Kouyaté stands by Conakry's firm line: “They mistook our pan-Africanism for weakness.” He cites sovereignty and public health, pointing to the damage caused by the cyanide used to extract gold [8].
Meeting in Ouagadougou on November 11 and 12, ministers of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES: Mali, Burkina, Niger) deplored “massive and uncoordinated” expulsions [7].

Key takeaway: Guinea wants to regain control of its gold, even if it means driving out tens of thousands of workers from neighboring countries, and the dispute is now spilling over into diplomacy and the media [1][3].

The crackdown is economic. In June 2026, Conakry had already banned exports of raw gold, to force it to be refined locally [9]. Shutting down illegal gold panning in Siguiri also means routing production through channels the state controls and taxes [5][9].

For Burkina, the abrupt return of more than 76,000 people is a social shock: these miners lose their income and must be reintegrated [1]. The Burkinabe government is in fact calling for support for them [1].
The crisis is testing a rapprochement between military regimes. AES countries are trying to repatriate their nationals without breaking with Conakry, while the war of words escalates [7][4].

Part of the gold sold worldwide comes from artisanal mines like those in Siguiri. When a producing country closes sites or requires refining at home, it changes who makes money on every gram, and thousands of families lose their income.

AI crash: money flees to US Treasuries, the yen and the Swiss franc, and the 10-year yield falls back below 5%

On Friday, November 20, as stocks plunged, investors rushed into safe havens. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury fell about 0.1 point to 4.94%, and both the yen and the Swiss franc gained 0.6% against the dollar [1][2][4].

US Treasury yields fell sharply as the drop in stocks pushed investors toward these investments seen as safe, according to CNBC [1]. During the session, the 10-year yield was down more than 0.07 point at 4.974% [1].
At the close, it fell to 4.94%, down 0.10 point on the day, according to Trading Economics [2]; ETF Trends puts it at 4.92% [3]. It was still above 5% the day before [2].
The Japanese yen and the Swiss franc, two traditional safe-haven currencies, gained 0.6% against the dollar, and the Bloomberg Dollar Index fell 0.2%, according to Bloomberg [4].
The day before, the dollar had risen on optimism around Anthropic's stock market listing: the AI rout erased part of that move [4].

Over the week, the yen gained against the seven other major currencies, even though Japanese growth and inflation disappointed, according to Babypips, which attributes this to the search for safety and speculation about a Bank of Japan rate hike [5].

The dollar limited its losses, as markets still see a Fed rate hike in December as almost certain [5]. Fed Governor Christopher Waller is even arguing for a half-point hike at the December 8–9 meeting [6].

Key takeaway: when fear takes hold, investors sell what is risky (AI stocks) and buy what can't go bust, or almost: US government debt, and the currencies of major creditor countries such as Japan and Switzerland [1][4].

This reflex has a concrete effect: by buying bonds massively, investors push their yields down. And the US 10-year yield serves as a benchmark for US mortgages and influences interest rates around the world [1][2].

The paradox of the week: the Fed is preparing to raise rates to curb inflation [6], but stock market panic is pushing them down in the markets. If the stock slide continues, markets could bet on a more cautious Fed.

A drop in US interest rates often ends up partly feeding through to European rates, and therefore to mortgage rates in France. A stronger yen also makes a trip to Japan more expensive for you, but makes Japanese products slightly cheaper.

How it works: why a bond's yield falls when everyone buys it

A bond is a loan: the US government promises to pay a fixed interest amount every year, then to repay the principal. The bond is then traded on the markets. When many investors want to buy it, its price rises. But the interest paid does not change: relative to a higher price, it therefore represents a lower return. That is why a flood of buyers seeking safety pushes down the 10-year “yield,” here by about 0.1 point in a single day [2]. The yen and the Swiss franc play a similar role: in a crisis, investors bring their money home or buy these currencies seen as solid, which makes them rise [4].

A crisis can reverse rate bets within days: markets then believed the Fed's hikes were over.

Oil: despite a Houthi missile on Riyadh, Brent posts its third weekly decline, at $92.57

On Friday, November 20, Brent rose 0.6% to $92.57 a barrel after the Houthi rebels' attack on Riyadh. But over the week, it lost 3.4% and US crude WTI 5.2%: a third weekly decline, as markets expect a global supply surplus [1][2].
The January Brent contract, Europe's benchmark, closed at $92.57 a barrel, up about 0.6% on the day [1].
US WTI (December contract) ended at $83.98, up $0.77 (+0.93%) [1].
Over the week, WTI lost 5.17% and Brent 3.41%, their third straight weekly decline [1].
Friday's rise came from Houthi attacks on Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, which revived supply concerns [2].
Analysts nevertheless expect global oil inventories to rise, with production growing faster than demand in the short term [1].
Investors are also watching the next meeting of OPEC+, the alliance of major producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia [3].
In India, a major importer, the fall in oil prices is one of the reasons for the stock market's rise this week, according to Reuters [4].
Key takeaway: in the oil market, fear of a surplus currently outweighs fear of war. A missile on Riyadh lifts prices for a few hours, but not enough to erase the downward trend [1][2].
The AI crash also plays a role: when markets fear an economic slowdown, they expect fewer trucks, planes and factories running, and therefore less oil consumed.

For importing countries such as India, France or Japan, a barrel at $92 rather than nearly $120 eases the energy bill and inflation [4]. For Saudi Arabia, whose budget depends on oil, it is the opposite.

The price of a barrel feeds through to diesel and gasoline prices at the pump with a lag of a few weeks. Three weeks of decline are rather good news for filling your tank, provided the war in the Middle East does not cut off deliveries.

How it works: why oil is falling despite a war

The price of oil depends on the balance between what is produced and what is consumed, but also on what markets expect. An attack on a major producer raises fears of a supply disruption: the price rises, as it did on Friday [2]. But if global inventories increase because production exceeds demand [1], buyers know there will be enough barrels, and sellers have to lower their prices. A war-related “risk premium” is added to the price, then melts away if deliveries continue despite the attacks.

news.2026-11-21-coree-du-sud-lee-examens: South Korea: after AI cheating reaching even the college entrance exam, President Lee orders a “from A to Z” overhaul of all national exams

On Friday, November 20, the day after the major university entrance exam, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung ordered a complete overhaul of national exams to fight cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, which he called a “serious criminal act” [1][2].
At a meeting with his senior advisers, Lee Jae-myung called for technologies to detect and block cheating, tighter surveillance in exam centers and severe penalties [1][2].
He wants investigations conducted with AI companies and a dedicated task force [1]. The overhaul is to cover the college entrance exam (CSAT), national certifications and private-sector hiring [2].
AI-equipped glasses were spotted during the CSAT, and the top scorer on the tax accountant exam admitted to cheating with generative AI [2].
The same day, a Gallup Korea poll conducted November 17–19 among 1,001 adults gave the president a 40% approval rating, one point higher than the previous week, and 49% disapproval [3][4].
Key takeaway: in a country where competitive exams determine careers, AI cheating threatens trust in the entire selection system [1][2].
Diplomacy remains Lee Jae-myung's main strength in the polls; the economy and purchasing power are the main source of discontent [3].
France is also wondering how to monitor its exams in the age of AI: South Korea's response, combining detection and criminal penalties, will be closely watched.
